title: Finding Yourself in a Map With Particles: A Cloud of Guesses, Weighed by What the Lidar Would See From Each, and the Room That Looks the Same From Two Places

questions.question: Why use many guesses instead of one estimate with an error bar?
options: Particles are cheaper than a Kalman filter
Particles do not need a map
A robot that does not know where it is may be in many places at once, which one estimate cannot say
questions.explanation: At the start the robot could be anywhere, and in a symmetric room it may be in one of two places. A cloud can hold both.

questions.question: Three thousand particles found the robot to:
questions.explanation: Spread over a 10 by 6 m room, the cloud of 3000 closed on the robot within five moves of 0.2 m.

questions.question: Of 10 runs, 50 particles lost the robot how many times?
questions.explanation: With so few particles none starts near the truth, and the cloud settles somewhere else. With 3000 the robot was never lost.

questions.question: In a room with nothing in it, the mirror image was taken for the robot in how many of 8 runs?
questions.explanation: From (2, 2) the bare room looks exactly as it does from (8, 4) facing the other way. A partition and a post took it to 0.

questions.question: Why is there a uniform share in the likelihood of a beam?
options: To make the weights add to one
To keep the cloud spread out
One wild beam (a person walking by) must not give a good particle a weight of zero
questions.explanation: The weight is a product over the beams. Without a floor, a single beam that hits a passer-by multiplies a good particle's weight by nearly nothing.

questions.question: Why can the mean of a cloud with two clumps be nowhere?
questions.explanation: With half the cloud at each of two places the average is a point in the middle where no particle is.
